title: AI-exposed college majors face a weaker and lower-paid first step into work
source_unit: Census Bureau Center for Economic Studies working paper using administrative records on college graduates and major-level labor-market AI exposure

observations.period: Post-ChatGPT labor-market entry; paper published September 2026

denominator.unit: study-defined graduate and major-exposure groups; exact public abstract denominator not disclosed

initial_employment_change.unit: percentage points for the most AI-exposed decile of majors

full_quarter_initial_earnings_change.unit: percent for the most AI-exposed decile of majors

earnings_pathway.value: about half of the decline came from lower earnings within sectors and the remainder from shifting toward lower-wage sectors such as restaurants and retail
earnings_pathway.unit: reported decomposition of initial earnings change

later_path.value: effects attenuated farther from labor-market entry but remained substantial for the most exposed majors

observations.method: Census CES working paper using administrative records on college graduates, major-level measures of labor-market AI exposure, and regression-adjusted comparisons before and after large language models became available. The paper studies employment, earnings, and job switching around the introduction of ChatGPT.
observations.uncertainty: This is a Census working paper and has not undergone the review and editorial process of an official Census publication. The public abstract does not provide all sample construction, exposure-measure, specification, or subgroup details. The estimates identify divergence associated with the study design; they do not by themselves establish that ChatGPT caused every affected outcome or identify each graduate's experience.
observations.subgroup: College graduates, compared by major-level labor-market AI exposure; the key reported comparison is the most exposed decile versus less-exposed majors.
observations.counterinterpretation: The pattern could reflect broader post-2022 sector demand, occupation or major selection, hiring freezes, macroeconomic changes, or how AI exposure is measured, in addition to AI-related changes in employer demand. Lower initial earnings can later recover and do not establish lifetime earnings, household security, job quality, or worker bargaining power.

related_sources.claim: The Census working-paper catalog identifies the paper as a September 2026 working paper and summarizes its initial employment and earnings estimates.

boundary: This record adds a bounded entry-to-work and early-earnings result for AI-exposed college majors. It does not establish permanent job displacement, a causal effect for every graduate, lifetime earnings, household wellbeing, political response, or whether education remains valuable over the full career.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Census paper landing page and official working-paper catalog reviewed; underlying restricted administrative records are not retained
